mcqs.q: Dental plaque is best described as:
opts: A structured, resilient biofilm that adheres tenaciously and is not removed by rinsing
A soft deposit easily washed off with a water spray
A salivary film containing no bacteria
mcqs.explain: Plaque is a structured biofilm; materia alba washes off; calculus is mineralized plaque.

mcqs.q: Materia alba differs from plaque in that it:
opts: Is loosely adherent and can be flushed off with a water spray
mcqs.explain: Materia alba is a soft, loosely adherent mixture of bacteria, debris and cells, removable by water spray.

opts: Mineralized plaque covered by a living plaque layer
mcqs.explain: Calculus is calcified plaque; its rough surface is always covered by a layer of viable plaque.

mcqs.q: Approximately what proportion of the SOLID component of plaque is bacteria?
mcqs.explain: Bacteria make up ~70–80% of plaque solids (plaque is ~80% water overall); 1 mg ≈ 250 million bacteria.

mcqs.q: The FIRST event in plaque formation is:
mcqs.explain: The acquired pellicle forms first, then initial adhesion, then colonization/maturation.

mcqs.q: Marginal supragingival plaque is clinically important because it:
opts: Lies at the gingival margin and is the key initiator of gingivitis
Is located deep within the periodontal pocket
Cannot be stained by disclosing agents
mcqs.explain: Supragingival plaque is coronal (tooth) or marginal (at the gingival margin); marginal plaque drives gingival inflammation.

mcqs.q: Subgingival plaque, being within the sulcus/pocket, is:
opts: Usually thin and not detectable by direct observation — found by running a probe around the margin
Thick and easily seen without a probe
mcqs.explain: Subgingival plaque is thin and hidden; its presence is detected by probing the margin.

mcqs.q: Tooth-associated (attached) subgingival plaque is dominated by:
opts: Gram-positive cocci, rods and filamentous bacteria
mcqs.explain: Attached (tooth-associated) plaque resembles supragingival plaque — Gram-positive cocci/rods/filaments; it is linked to calculus and root caries/resorption.

opts: Lacks an interbacterial matrix and is rich in Gram-negative rods, flagellated bacteria and spirochetes
Is firmly attached with abundant matrix
mcqs.explain: Loosely adherent, matrix-poor plaque in direct contact with the epithelium; predominantly Gram-negative, flagellated and spirochetal.

mcqs.q: The main 'bridging' organism linking early and late colonizers is:
mcqs.explain: F. nucleatum coaggregates with both early (Strep/Actinomyces) and late colonizers, bridging the two.

mcqs.q: Primary (early) colonizers of the tooth surface are mainly:
mcqs.explain: Early colonizers are predominantly Gram-positive Streptococcus and Actinomyces.

mcqs.q: S. sanguis can antagonize A. actinomycetemcomitans by producing:
mcqs.explain: S. sanguis produces H₂O₂, which can kill A. actinomycetemcomitans — a beneficial antagonistic interaction.

mcqs.q: Socransky's 'red complex' (most associated with periodontitis) comprises:
opts: P. gingivalis, T. forsythia and T. denticola
S. sanguinis, S. mitis and A. oris
F. nucleatum, P. intermedia and P. micra
mcqs.explain: The red complex = P. gingivalis, Tannerella forsythia, Treponema denticola — the most pathogenic cluster.

mcqs.q: In the older 'localized aggressive periodontitis', which organism may comprise up to 90% of the cultivable microbiota?
mcqs.explain: A. actinomycetemcomitans predominates in localized aggressive periodontitis (up to ~90%).

mcqs.q: Necrotizing ulcerative gingivitis (NUG) is associated with high proportions of:
mcqs.explain: NUG shows abundant spirochetes and F. nucleatum (fusospirochetal complex).

mcqs.q: The NONSPECIFIC plaque hypothesis holds that periodontal disease results from:
opts: The noxious products of the entire plaque flora (total quantity)
A keystone pathogen at low abundance
mcqs.explain: Nonspecific hypothesis = disease from the whole plaque mass; specific hypothesis = particular pathogens; ecological/keystone are later refinements.

opts: P. gingivalis, even in low numbers, remodels a benign microbiota into a dysbiotic one
Only the total amount of plaque matters
Bacteria play no role in periodontitis
mcqs.explain: P. gingivalis acts as a low-abundance keystone pathogen, driving dysbiosis and disease.

mcqs.q: Which best defines dysbiosis in the periodontal context?
opts: A shift of the resident microbiota from a balanced/benign community to a disease-associated one
mcqs.explain: Dysbiosis is an imbalance of the microbial community favoring pathogens, driven by environmental change/keystone pathogens.

saqs.q: Differentiate dental plaque, materia alba and calculus.
saqs.a: Dental plaque is a structured, resilient biofilm (~70–80% bacteria in a matrix) that adheres tenaciously and is not removed by rinsing. Materia alba is a soft, loosely adherent accumulation of bacteria, food debris and cells that can be flushed off with a water spray. Calculus is mineralized (calcified) plaque, always covered by a layer of living plaque, and acts as a plaque-retentive surface.

saqs.q: Describe the three stages of plaque formation.
saqs.a: 1) Acquired pellicle — a thin salivary glycoprotein film coats the tooth within minutes. 2) Initial adhesion and attachment — bacteria bind to the pellicle. 3) Colonization and maturation — bacterial growth, coaggregation and development of a mature biofilm.

saqs.q: Compare tooth-associated and epithelium-associated subgingival plaque.
saqs.a: Tooth-associated (attached) subgingival plaque resembles supragingival plaque — dominated by Gram-positive cocci, rods and filaments, with a matrix, and is associated with calculus formation, root caries and root resorption. Epithelium-associated (unattached) plaque is loosely adherent, lacks an interbacterial matrix, lies in direct contact with the sulcular/junctional epithelium, and is dominated by Gram-negative rods and cocci, flagellated bacteria and spirochetes.

saqs.q: Explain bacterial colonization of the biofilm, naming primary colonizers, the bridging organism and late colonizers.
saqs.a: Primary (early) colonizers are mainly Gram-positive Streptococcus and Actinomyces species (e.g. S. sanguinis, S. mitis, A. naeslundii). Fusobacterium nucleatum is the key bridging organism that coaggregates with both early and late colonizers. Secondary (late) colonizers are Gram-negative anaerobes such as P. gingivalis, T. forsythia, T. denticola, P. intermedia and Capnocytophaga.

saqs.q: Outline the evolution of plaque-disease hypotheses.
saqs.a: Nonspecific plaque hypothesis — disease results from the noxious products of the entire plaque flora (total quantity). Specific plaque hypothesis — only specific pathogens cause disease (qualitative composition). Ecological plaque hypothesis — an environmental change (e.g. increased GCF, pH, inflammation) causes an ecological shift that selects pathogens. Keystone-pathogen hypothesis — a low-abundance keystone pathogen (P. gingivalis) remodels a benign microbiota into a dysbiotic community that causes disease.
